cards.answer: I built it because every scheduled workflow on our Linux analytics server needed one place to answer a single question: did it run, and did it work? The monitor is custom, designed from scratch for the Advanced Analytics environment rather than adopted off the shelf, and it covers the role I'd otherwise get from MLflow run tracking plus Airflow alerting. The design choice that makes it work is a standard log schema: each pipeline writes Parquet logs in the same shape, and one monitor reads all of them. It is deployed and runs on a cron schedule in production, with no manual steps.

cards.title: Job monitor: module layout

cards.answer: The monitor is a modular Python application with one file per concern. log_reader.py loads and concatenates the pipeline Parquet logs into a single DataFrame. alert_rules.py classifies failures by status and age. time_windows.py holds the silence detection and the reusable last_n_hours and last_n_days filters. emailer.py builds and sends the alert mail. config.py holds the settings, including the list of extra log paths, and main.py runs the whole check. Keeping them apart means I can change a rule, such as a silence threshold, without touching how logs are read or mail is sent.

cards.answer: Onboarding a pipeline takes no new monitor code. Pipelines under the standard pipelines directory are discovered automatically, and one living elsewhere, such as the proposal processing pipeline, is registered by adding its log path to an EXTRA_LOG_FILES list in config.py. The current list names pipeline_demo, which is auto-discovered, and proposal_processing, which is registered that way. I also onboarded the quarterly workforce planning pipeline with a per-pipeline silence override. Because the logging contract is shared, any future pipeline built on it is monitorable from day one.

cards.title: Job monitor: unreadable logs as failures
questions: what is LOG_READ_FAILED in the job monitor
what happens if a pipeline log file is corrupt
how does the monitor handle broken parquet log files
who monitors the logs themselves in the job monitoring app
synthetic failure records in the monitor
what if the log file cannot be read by the job monitor
LOG_READ_FAILED status explained
corrupt log file alert in the pipeline monitor
does a broken log hide a failing pipeline
how does the job monitor surface logging infrastructure failures
unreadable log file permission error monitoring
cards.answer: An unreadable log is treated as a failure, not skipped. If a pipeline's Parquet log is broken, corrupt or unreadable, the monitor writes a synthetic LOG_READ_FAILED record for it, so the problem shows up as an alert instead of the pipeline silently dropping out of view. It is tiered with real failures: LOG_READ_FAILED within the last 24 hours is CRITICAL, like a FAILED stage. The reasoning is simple. A monitor that quietly ignores logs it can't read would go blind exactly when the logging layer breaks, and the file path stored on each row helps me diagnose corruption or permission problems.

cards.answer: The email is written so someone can start debugging from the inbox. It opens with the subject line '!!! Pipeline Alert !!!' for visibility. Each CRITICAL failure lists the pipeline, stage, error type, error message, run ID and timestamp, plus a traceback preview. Each silent pipeline lists its last successful run and the hours elapsed. WARNING and INFO rows ride along as context when a CRITICAL fires. Mail goes out through the server's local sendmail because outbound SMTP isn't available there, and a send_test_email function lets me validate the emailer on its own, without running the full monitoring logic.

cards.answer: I built two notebooks as the human inspection layer, so triage never needs a live alert. log_reader_sanity_check.ipynb documents the log schema column by column and explains how to tell root failures from cascades, how silent pipelines are found and how time-window checks feed the alerts. monitor_investigation.ipynb exposes every monitor function across 10 sections: load logs, last 24 hours, all failures, root failures only, the latest full traceback, alert classification preview, silent pipeline detection, last success per pipeline, email body preview and full run history. They double as living documentation of the logic.

cards.answer: The monitor only sees pipelines that write the standard Parquet log, so a job outside the contract is invisible to it. Alerts go by email, and only CRITICAL severity sends one, so a stale WARNING or INFO appears only as context in a later message. It is meant to run on cron every 30 to 60 minutes, so detection is bounded by that cadence rather than being instant. My notes carry no count of incidents it has caught, so I won't offer one. What I can show is the design: absence detection, cascade separation and visible log failures. For the quarterly pipeline I also added matching Grafana panel targets and threshold guidance.

cards.answer: I wrote it up as a Medium article titled 'I Got Tired of Pipelines Failing Silently, So I Built My Own Monitoring System'. The project matters beyond the tool itself. Monitoring and pipeline health tracking sit outside a data scientist's normal scope, and building them meant owning the platform and the production governance layer, not only the pipelines. Because of the standardized logging contract, every future pipeline is monitorable from day one, so the capability grows with the platform instead of needing custom work per pipeline.

cards.answer: I replaced manual and semi-manual legacy workflows for CPA and PUA payroll data with a fully automated end-to-end ETL pipeline. The result: processing time dropped from hours to minutes, with better reliability, repeatability and governance. It was built for University Payroll & Benefits and the System Office. The pipeline reads raw payroll Excel files, applies business-rule mappings, deduplication and derived-field logic, and produces clean, analytics-ready outputs. Status is near-final, with the production transition underway, so I'd call it close to done rather than long established.

It ingests the raw payroll Excel files, applies the business-rule mappings, removes duplicates, calculates the derived fields and writes clean, analytics-ready outputs. Putting the rules in a framework is what replaced the legacy approach, where the work was manual or semi-manual. My notes don't list the individual mapping rules or row volumes, so I can describe the structure but not those specifics.

cards.answer: The pipeline decides for itself whether a file is CPA or PUA, based on the file's naming convention. That removes manual configuration, so nobody has to tell the system which kind of payroll file they uploaded, and it reduces operational risk because there is no setting for anyone to get wrong. I treat it as a design principle: if a human choice can be inferred from something already reliable, infer it. The trade-off is that detection depends on people following the naming convention, and my notes don't describe how a misnamed file is handled.

I operationalized the workflow with GitHub Actions, which gives one-click execution with no local environment setup. cards.answer: Every output the payroll pipeline writes is timestamped and versioned, which supports auditability, traceability and repeatable downstream analysis. If someone asks how a number was produced, the run can be identified, traced and repeated instead of reconstructed from memory. That is the governance side of the project, alongside the speed gain from hours to minutes. Payroll is data where being able to explain a result matters as much as producing it quickly. What I can't give you from my notes is a formal audit outcome, because the project is near-final and still in its production transition.

cards.answer: It's a Streamlit job matching prototype for UIS HR that uses BERT embeddings and FAISS for context-aware semantic search across job descriptions. Behind it I built several classification pipelines and used generative AI to expand job summaries and reduce classification redundancy. Status is delivered, and I'd call it a prototype, not a production system. The point of the semantic approach is that a search for a role finds descriptions that mean the same thing even when the wording differs, which keyword search misses. My notes hold no accuracy figures, so I don't quote any.

cards.title: Job classification app: BERT embeddings and FAISS search
questions: how does the job matching app use BERT and FAISS

what is the retrieval design in the UIS HR job matching prototype
cards.answer: Job descriptions are turned into BERT embeddings and indexed with FAISS, so the Streamlit app can retrieve descriptions by meaning rather than shared words. That matters in HR, where the same work can appear under different titles and phrasing. FAISS handles fast nearest-neighbor lookup over the vectors. I used the same embedding-plus-FAISS pattern at much larger scale in the procurement system, with 5.19 million vectors. For this prototype my notes don't give the corpus size, the exact BERT variant or retrieval metrics, so I can explain the design but not quantify it.
